lab_title: VSEPR Theory: Predicting Three-Dimensional Molecular Shapes
top_level_objectives: Use Lewis structures to identify electron domains around a central atom.
Predict electron-domain geometry from the number of electron domains using VSEPR theory.
Distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular geometry when lone pairs are present.
Explain how lone pairs alter bond angles relative to ideal geometries.
Compare VSEPR predictions with common molecular examples such as H2O, NH3, CH4, PF5, SF6, and XeF4.

scenes.scene_name: 1. From Lewis Structure to Electron Domains
scenes.brief_purpose: Introduce the workflow from a 2D Lewis structure to the 3D regions of electron density used in VSEPR predictions.
key_visuals: A flat Lewis structure panel for a simple molecule such as methane or water.
Highlighted bonding pairs and lone pairs around the central atom.
A central atom with movable electron-domain markers appearing around it in AR.
student_actions: Select the central atom in the Lewis structure.
Tap bonds and lone pairs to classify each as an electron domain.
Count the total number of electron domains before moving to the 3D model.

scenes.brief_purpose: Show the central VSEPR idea: electron domains spread out in space to minimize mutual repulsion.
key_visuals: Electron-domain spheres around a central atom pushing away from one another.
Animated motion from crowded arrangements to stable symmetric arrangements.
Angle labels appearing between domains as the arrangement settles.
student_actions: Drag electron domains into different starting positions.
Release them and observe how they move to reduce repulsion.
Compare the final angles for two, three, and four electron domains.

scenes.brief_purpose: Build the complete set of ideal electron-domain geometries used as the foundation for VSEPR.
key_visuals: Side-by-side AR models of linear, trigonal planar, tetrahedral, trigonal bipyramidal, and octahedral arrangements.
Color-coded domains around a central atom.
Ideal bond-angle labels such as 180°, 120°, 109.5°, 90°, and 120° where appropriate.
student_actions: Step through models with 2, 3, 4, 5, and 6 electron domains.
Rotate each geometry to view its true 3D shape.
Match each domain count to the correct electron-domain geometry name.

scenes.scene_name: 4. Molecular Geometry with Lone Pairs: 2–4 Domains
scenes.brief_purpose: Distinguish electron-domain geometry from molecular shape using common examples with lone pairs in smaller domain sets.
key_visuals: Tetrahedral electron-domain framework transitioning into methane, ammonia, and water molecular shapes.
Lone pairs shown as translucent larger clouds compared with bonding pairs.
Labels for tetrahedral, trigonal pyramidal, and bent shapes.
student_actions: Hide lone-pair clouds to see the molecular geometry formed by atoms only.
Compare CH4, NH3, and H2O within the same tetrahedral electron-domain arrangement.
Measure or read bond-angle changes from 109.5° in methane to smaller angles in ammonia and water.

scenes.scene_name: 5. Lone Pairs in Expanded Octets: 5–6 Domains
scenes.brief_purpose: Explore how lone pairs modify trigonal bipyramidal and octahedral electron-domain geometries to form additional common shapes.
key_visuals: Trigonal bipyramidal framework showing equatorial and axial positions.
Models of seesaw and T-shaped geometries formed by placing lone pairs in preferred positions.
Octahedral framework transitioning to square pyramidal and square planar shapes.
student_actions: Place lone pairs into trigonal bipyramidal and octahedral frameworks.
Observe which positions minimize repulsion and why they are favored.
Identify the resulting molecular geometries after lone pairs are hidden.

scenes.brief_purpose: Connect VSEPR predictions to real molecular examples and reinforce the prediction process.
key_visuals: AR gallery of H2O, NH3, CH4, PF5, SF6, and XeF4 models.
Cards showing Lewis structure, electron-domain count, electron-domain geometry, molecular geometry, and approximate bond angles.
Overlay comparison between idealized VSEPR shapes and observed molecular structures.
student_actions: Choose a molecule and predict its electron-domain and molecular geometry before revealing the answer.
Rotate and inspect each real-molecule model.
Complete a final matching activity linking formulas to shapes and bond-angle trends.
